overview.text: The Bulavin Rebellion was an uprising centered on the Don Cossacks during Peter the Great’s reign. The Russian government sought firmer control of the Don region and wanted fugitive serfs returned to their landlords. A 1707 order for a census and a military expedition to seize escapees helped spark resistance under the Cossack leader Kondratiy Bulavin. His followers killed the commander of that expedition in October 1707 and later captured Cherkassk, the Don’s political center. The movement did not unite all Cossacks: some remained loyal to the tsar. Bulavin died during a confrontation with opponents in July 1708, and government forces suppressed the revolt, though Cossack customs survived.

key_facts.text: The revolt is usually dated 1707–1708.
Peter the Great ordered a census of Cossack settlements in July 1707 to locate fugitive serfs.
Bulavin’s rebels killed the commander Dolgorukiy in October 1707.
In 1708 the rebels took Cherkassk, the Don Cossack political center.
Bulavin was killed in a July 1708 shootout with Cossack opponents.

overview.text: The Peace of Westphalia was a set of 1648 agreements ending the Thirty Years’ War within the Holy Roman Empire. The emperor and his allies made separate treaties with Sweden at Osnabrück and France at Münster after years of negotiation. The settlement redistributed territory and confirmed the political rights of the empire’s princes and other estates, including a limited right to make alliances abroad. It also extended legal recognition from Catholicism and Lutheranism to the Reformed faith and used conditions in 1624 to settle many disputes over church property. Westphalia shaped the empire’s politics for generations, but its princes still remained within an imperial constitutional order.

key_facts.text: The emperor’s treaties with Sweden and France were signed at Osnabrück and Münster in 1648.
The peace settled the Thirty Years’ War within the Holy Roman Empire.
The Reformed faith gained recognition alongside Catholicism and Lutheranism.
January 1, 1624 served as a benchmark for contested ecclesiastical property.
Imperial estates could make foreign alliances only within treaty limits that protected the empire.

overview.text: Jean-Baptiste Colbert was a powerful minister of France’s Louis XIV, responsible for finance and many other state offices. He promoted commerce, royal manufacturing, shipping, and overseas trading companies as ways to strengthen the monarchy. His name became associated with “Colbertism,” an economic approach using state direction and protection of domestic production. Colbert also supported science: he founded the Academy of Sciences in 1666, and its first members met in the king’s Paris library. His legacy includes colonial slavery. At Louis XIV’s request, he helped initiate the ordinance later called the Code Noir; after Colbert died in 1683, a commission drafted it under his son’s supervision, and it was issued in 1685.

key_facts.text: Colbert served Louis XIV as controller general of finances.
He promoted trading companies, including the French East India Company.
He established the Academy of Sciences in 1666.
The Academy’s first meeting was on December 22, 1666, in the king’s library.
The 1685 colonial slavery ordinance was initiated with Colbert but drafted after his death under his son’s supervision.

overview.text: Amarna is the modern name for the Egyptian site where Pharaoh Akhenaten built a new royal city called Akhetaten, meaning “Horizon of the Aten.” In the fifth year of his reign he chose this place beside the Nile for palaces and temples dedicated to the Aten, the sun disk central to his religious reforms. Its central district held major temples, a palace, and administrative buildings. The city was occupied for only a short period; after Akhenaten’s death, Tutankhamun left it and much of it was abandoned. Archaeologists also found diplomatic letters there, written in cuneiform on clay tablets and exchanged with rulers beyond Egypt.

key_facts.text: Akhenaten named the city Akhetaten, “Horizon of the Aten.”
He selected the site in the fifth year of his reign.
The Central City had two main Aten temples and the principal state palace.
The city was largely abandoned after the royal court left under Tutankhamun.
An Amarna tablet records a letter from the Assyrian king Ashur-uballit to Egypt’s king.

overview.text: At the Battle of Stamford Bridge on September 25, 1066, England’s King Harold Godwinson defeated an invading Norwegian army near York. Harald Hardrada, king of Norway, had joined forces with Harold’s brother Tostig, and they had captured York before the English king hurried north. The English attack killed both Hardrada and Tostig, although Norwegian reinforcements nearly reversed the battle before Harold’s troops prevailed. This victory removed one claimant’s army, but it came during a wider succession crisis: William of Normandy was preparing another invasion in the south. Harold soon faced William at Hastings, making Stamford Bridge one of two defining English battles of 1066.

The Norwegian leader was King Harald Hardrada.
Hardrada allied with Tostig, the English king’s brother.
Both Hardrada and Tostig died in the English victory.

overview.text: The Beaver Wars, also called the Iroquois Wars, were recurring seventeenth-century conflicts involving the Haudenosaunee Five Nations, neighboring Indigenous peoples, and European allies in northeastern North America. The fur trade mattered: access to beaver pelts and trade routes affected alliances with Dutch and French merchants. Yet historians warn against treating fur as the only cause. Epidemic losses, the taking and adoption of captives, diplomacy, and competition for influence also shaped the fighting. Haudenosaunee attacks helped break up the Wendat homeland in the late 1640s, and many Wendat people fled or joined other communities. These wars transformed Indigenous and colonial relationships across the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence regions.

key_facts.text: “Beaver Wars” is one name for the long-running Iroquois Wars.
The Haudenosaunee Five Nations were Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca.
The fur trade was one factor, but historians also examine mourning wars, epidemic losses, and political goals.

overview.text: Boris Godunov ruled Russia as tsar from 1598 until his death in 1605, near the beginning of the Time of Troubles. He had been the brother-in-law of Tsar Feodor, who died without a child and ended the Rurik dynasty’s direct line. Godunov faced doubts about his legitimacy amid social and political strain. Rumors accused him of involvement in the earlier death of Prince Dmitry, Feodor’s younger brother, but the accusation was never established. In 1604 a claimant saying he was Dmitry gathered opponents and entered Russia. The dynastic crisis continued after Boris died, and it ended only when Michael Romanov was chosen tsar in 1613.

key_facts.text: Godunov was tsar from 1598 to 1605.
He was the brother-in-law of Feodor, whose childless death ended the Rurik dynasty’s direct line.
Claims that Boris had Prince Dmitry murdered were rumors, not established fact.

overview.text: Algeria is a North African country whose modern independence followed more than a century of French rule. France conquered Algiers in 1830 and later incorporated coastal areas into French administrative departments. The Algerian War began in 1954 as the National Liberation Front, or FLN, fought for independence against French rule. Negotiations produced the Évian Accords in March 1962, setting a ceasefire and a transition toward Algerian sovereignty; violence did not stop immediately. Algerian voters chose independence in a July 1962 referendum, and France recognized the new state soon afterward. The history of Algeria’s independence involves colonialism, armed struggle, diplomacy, and the difficult aftermath of war.

The Algerian War began in 1954.
The FLN was the principal Algerian independence movement in the war.

overview.text: The Bansenshūkai is a Japanese compilation of ninjutsu knowledge associated with the Iga and Kōka traditions. It dates to 1676, during the Edo period, when manuals helped preserve techniques and ideas in an era with fewer opportunities for shinobi to practice wartime skills. The work discusses methods, tools, the history and meaning of ninjutsu, and the conduct expected of practitioners. It also draws on Sun Tzu’s Art of War, especially the value of intelligence and winning without direct battle. The compiler is traditionally identified as Fujibayashi Yasutake, although Iga City’s catalog notes that authorship is uncertain because the surviving copy names only the Fujibayashi family.

It compiles traditions associated with Iga and Kōka.

overview.text: The Khalistan movement seeks an independent Sikh homeland centered on Punjab in India. It grew from disputes about political power, Sikh identity, and regional autonomy, and gained force during the 1980s. Armed separatist groups fought the Indian state, while many Sikhs did not support militancy or independence. In June 1984 the Indian Army entered the Golden Temple complex at Amritsar, where militants had taken positions; the assault and its damage deeply angered many Sikhs. Later that year, the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was followed by organized anti-Sikh violence. Human Rights Watch documents abuses by both militants and Indian security forces. Support for Khalistan has also appeared among some Sikh communities outside India.

The movement was especially prominent in the 1980s and 1990s.
The Indian Army entered the Golden Temple complex in June 1984.
